newsitem.title: USA: U.S. property insurers face tough year in 1997.
newsitem.headline: U.S. property insurers face tough year in 1997.

text.p: U.S. property-casualty insurers are likely to see a slight decline in pre-tax operating income in 1997 and premium growth is expected to remain weak at 2.8 percent, according to a Standard & Poor's forecast.

Margins also are likely to be under pressure as loss costs and operating costs continue to increase at rates in excess of the growth in revenue, Standard & Poor's said in a forecast provided by the Insurance Information Institute.
Although pre-tax operating income is likely to decline, realized capital gains may make the bottom line net income acceptable to many insurers, S&P said.
The combined ratio, a key measure of profitability, will likely deteriorate slightly in 1997 to perhaps 106.7 percent and growth of investment income should be modest, S&P said.
The slow growth, highly competitive environment is likely to fuel additional mergers and acquisitions in 1997, S&P said.
"In a slow growth, highly competitive environment, many companies have concluded that the most economical path for growth is through a business combination," S&P said.
The sluggish 1997 outlook follows a lackluster 1996, the Insurance Information Institute said.
Premiums and claims both grew at the same pace of 3.2 percent from 1995 to 1996.
The industry's rate of return was estimated at 9.4 percent, up slightly from 9.0 percent in 1995, the Institute said.
Catastrophe losses were roughly similar for both years. Catastrophe loses were estimated at $7 billion in 1996, down from $8.3 billion in 1995.
The largest catastrophe in 1996 was Hurricane Fran, which cost the industry $1.6 billion.

Investiment income posted a slight 0.8 percent decline in 1996. But this was offset by a significant increase of 65 percent in realized capital gains, partially reflecting the strong bond and equity markets in 1996.
The net result was an 8.4 percent increase in investment gain in 1996.
